text: Before any new PySpark gets written, this lesson sketches the whole incremental redesign in plain English. Every layer -- Bronze, Silver, Gold -- changes in some way, but not equally and not for the same reason. Getting the plan straight now means the code in later lessons is just typing up a decision you've already made, instead of making the decision while also fighting syntax.

Start with Bronze. Today it re-reads every source file every night as part of rebuilding everything downstream. The new design gives Bronze a memory: a small tracking table called meta-dot-last-ingested-date. Every successful run records the latest source date it just loaded. The next run reads that value first, and only looks at files dated after it -- never the whole history. Bronze-dot-sales-raw stays append-only, exactly as before; what changes is that each run only touches what's genuinely new.

Silver changes the most. Today it gets dropped and rebuilt from Bronze on every run, which would throw away the whole win once Bronze is incremental. The fix is Delta Lake's merge-into: instead of rebuilding silver-dot-sales-clean, each run merges only the newly-ingested rows into it, matched on transaction-id, the table's true unique key. A genuinely new row gets inserted. A row that corrects an existing transaction -- a late fix, a re-sent file -- gets updated in place.

Here's the whole plan end to end, five steps. Read the watermark. Ingest only new files into Bronze. Merge those new rows into Silver on transaction-id. Rebuild both Gold tables from the now-current Silver table. Advance the watermark. That last step matters -- forget it, and the next run thinks nothing has ever been ingested.

And here's the part that surprises people: Gold barely changes. Both Gold tables still just read from Silver and aggregate it -- that logic doesn't need to become incremental the way Bronze and Silver do, because Silver itself is now small and current, not the entire history. The real change in Gold is simply that there are now two tables instead of one: gold-dot-daily-sales-summary, unchanged, for Store Operations, and the new gold-dot-category-breakdown, for the Regional Manager.

So that's the plan: Bronze learns what it's already seen, Silver merges instead of rebuilding, and Gold quietly becomes two tables instead of one, at no extra cost per run. Next lesson looks at exactly why the old full-reload design can't keep up anymore -- the real cost of reprocessing all of history every single night just to add one new day.
